chapter: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
title: Mixed patronage at the Coconut Grove and Culver City discrimination
summary: Brown was unaware of racial restrictions in Los Angeles, and says Sebastian kept Culver City officials on side.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: At the Coconut Grove were there a

mixed racial patronage, or not? I ask because when I worked there in 1950 the management kind of panicked at the thoughts that Lena Horne would draw a mixed crowd. They said, "We can't have that. We don't want anybody but white people in here."
Was that attitude the same then?

I wasn't aware of too much of that, because well in the first place, I didn't live out here. I was only visiting during the time that the band would come out here, or that I took my vacation and came out here to see my family, and so I didn't run into much of that at all. I was very surprised to hear that as much of it existed as they say did --
You were telling me something about Culver City. You said that Culver City wasn't good, that Frank Sebastián really ran the place.

Culver -- yes, Culver City really was very nasty, but Frank Sebastián, through his -- he was a big man all over California, and he pretty much had his way, and I know many times we would come to work or the -- before we came to work they would be a party there or a big dinner for the sheriff's department, and all those kind of things.
So kept it half-way cool. Yeah.
So anybody who wanted to could come to the Cotton Club, but not necessarily anywhere else in Culver City? Is that true?

No, they were sort of discriminatory. Of course you know one thing that makes it so stupid to begin with, that type of thing, is there have always been great numbers, many, many Negros, who are white as any white person, and they went where they pleased, so the very idea of setting up such a system was very stupid.
But such a system existed. At least I didn't in some areas and in some eras here. (Inaudible) know how it was effected and during that period in the late twenties and early thirties.
Well, I was -- as I say, I was never around it enough to really feel it, and I was rather surprised to find out later on that that condition had been here as strong as it was.
